question: Arrange the following carbocations
explanation: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl: more α-hydrogens (hyperconjugation) and more +I alkyl groups disperse the positive charge.

question: Arrange the following carbocations
explanation: Benzyl and allyl cations are resonance stabilised (benzyl more, as the charge is delocalised over the ring); the ethyl cation has only hyperconjugation; the vinyl cation has the positive charge on an sp carbon in an empty sp^2-like orbital orthogonal to the π bond, so it is very unstable.
trap: Vinyl and phenyl cations are NOT stabilised by the adjacent π system: the empty orbital is in the plane, perpendicular to the π cloud.

question: Arrange the following carbocations
explanation: Each phenyl group delocalises the charge into its ring: $\ce{(C6H5)3C+}$ (trityl) > $\ce{(C6H5)2CH+}$ > $\ce{C6H5CH2+}$ > a simple 1° alkyl cation.

question: Arrange the following para-substituted benzyl cations $\ce{p-X-C6H4-CH2+}$
explanation: +M of OCH3 is strongest (extra oxonium-type resonance structure), CH3 is +I/hyperconjugative, H is the reference, and NO2 (-M, -I) destabilises the cation most.

question: Arrange the following carbocations
explanation: The oxygen lone pair of $\ce{CH3OCH2+}$ donates into the empty p orbital (+M, octet-complete oxonium resonance form), making it more stable than the 3° cation; the rest follow 3° > 2° > 1°.
trap: An electronegative O attached to C+ looks destabilising (-I), but lone-pair donation (+M) outweighs it.

question: If an $\ce{-OCH3}$ group is introduced at the para position of the benzyl cation $\ce{C6H5CH2+}$, its stability
explanation: The para OCH3 lone pair is conjugated with the cationic centre through the ring (+M), giving an extra resonance structure with a C=O+ -type oxonium bond.

question: If an $\ce{-OCH3}$ group is introduced at the meta position of the benzyl cation $\ce{C6H5CH2+}$, its stability
explanation: At the meta position the OCH3 cannot conjugate with the benzylic carbon (the charge is delocalised only to ortho and para positions); only its -I effect operates, so the cation is slightly destabilised.
trap: Students assume OCH3 always stabilises a cation; +M acts only from ortho/para positions.

question: If a $\ce{-NO2}$ group is introduced at the para position of the benzyl cation $\ce{C6H5CH2+}$, its stability
explanation: NO2 withdraws electrons by -I and -M; it intensifies the positive charge and destabilises the cation.

question: Compare the stability of the two carbocations
explanation: In the p-methoxybenzyl cation the OCH3 lone pair delocalises the charge (+M); in the meta isomer only -I operates.

question: Compare the stability of the two carbocations
explanation: Benzyl cation is stabilised by resonance with the ring; in $\ce{C6H5CH2CH2+}$ the ring is insulated by a CH2 group, so it is only a 1° alkyl cation (it also tends to rearrange).

question: Which of the following carbocations is the most stable?
explanation: The cyclopropylmethyl cation is exceptionally stabilised by the 'bent' (banana) σ bonds of the cyclopropane ring overlapping with the empty p orbital (σ-conjugation, dancing resonance); it is more stable than a 3° alkyl or even a benzyl cation.
trap: Cyclopropylcarbinyl cation beats 2° and often 3° and benzyl cations; the ring strain/bent bonds give it π-like character.

question: Which of the following carbocations is aromatic and exceptionally stable?
explanation: The tropylium (cycloheptatrienyl) cation is planar, cyclic, fully conjugated with 6 π electrons (4n+2, n=1); it is stable enough to be isolated as a salt (e.g. tropylium bromide).

question: Arrange the following carbanions
explanation: Greater s-character holds the lone pair closer to the nucleus and stabilises the negative charge: sp > sp² > sp³.

question: Arrange the following carbanions
explanation: Alkyl groups (+I) intensify the negative charge, so stability falls from methyl to 3°.
trap: This is the reverse of carbocation order.

question: Arrange the following carbanions
explanation: Each phenyl group delocalises the negative charge: trityl > diphenylmethyl > benzyl > ethyl (pKa of the conjugate acids ~31, ~32, ~41, ~50).

question: Arrange the following carbanions (conjugate bases of the carbon acids)
explanation: Stability follows the acidity of the parent C-H: nitromethane (pKa ~10) > acetone (~19) > acetonitrile (~25) > ethane (~50).

question: Arrange the following carbanions
explanation: Stability follows the pKa of the parent hydrocarbon: cyclopentadiene ~16 (aromatic anion) < indene ~20 < fluorene ~23 < triphenylmethane ~31.

question: If a $\ce{-NO2}$ group is introduced at the para position of the benzyl carbanion $\ce{C6H5CH2^-}$, its stability
explanation: NO2 withdraws electrons (-I, -M) and the charge is delocalised onto the nitro oxygens via the ring.

question: If a methyl group replaces one H on the carbanionic carbon of $\ce{CH3^-}$, giving $\ce{CH3CH2^-}$, its stability
explanation: The +I methyl group pushes electron density onto the already electron-rich carbon, increasing charge density and decreasing stability.

question: If an $\ce{-OCH3}$ group is introduced at the para position of the benzyl carbanion $\ce{C6H5CH2^-}$, its stability
explanation: The +M lone pair pushes electron density towards the carbanionic centre (ring positions bearing the negative charge), destabilising the anion.
trap: +M groups stabilise cations but destabilise anions.

question: Compare the stability of the two carbanions
explanation: Cycloheptatrienyl anion would have 8 π electrons (antiaromatic if planar); the cyclopentadienyl anion has 6π (aromatic). Corresponding acids: cyclopentadiene pKa ~16, cycloheptatriene ~36.

question: Compare the stability of the two carbanions
explanation: The sp carbanion (50% s) holds its lone pair closer to the nucleus than the sp³ carbanion (25% s).

question: Cyclopentadiene (pKa ~16) is far more acidic than cyclohepta-1,3,5-triene (pKa ~36) because
options: It has less ring strain than cycloheptatriene
explanation: Loss of H+ from cyclopentadiene gives an aromatic cyclopentadienyl anion (6π, planar, cyclic); the cycloheptatrienyl anion has 8π and would be antiaromatic.

question: Arrange the following free radicals
explanation: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl (hyperconjugation with α C-H bonds, +I); vinyl radical is least stable among alkyl-type due to sp character of the radical centre in σ orbital.

question: Arrange the following free radicals
explanation: Allyl radical is resonance stabilised and more stable than 3° alkyl, which in turn > 2° > 1°.

question: Arrange the following radicals
explanation: Each phenyl group delocalises the unpaired electron; $\ce{(C6H5)3C.}$ (Gomberg's trityl radical) is so stable it exists in solution.

question: Arrange the following C-H bonds
explanation: Weaker C-H bond means more stable radical formed: vinyl C-H (~111 kcal/mol) > methane (~105) > 3° C-H (~96) > allylic C-H (~88).
trap: BDE order is the reverse of radical stability order.

question: If a methyl group replaces one H on the radical carbon of the ethyl radical $\ce{CH3CH2.}$, forming isopropyl radical, its stability
explanation: More α-C-H bonds for hyperconjugation: 2° > 1°.

question: If a phenyl group replaces one H of the methyl radical $\ce{CH3.}$, forming benzyl radical, its stability
explanation: The unpaired electron is delocalised over ortho and para positions of the ring.

question: Compare the stability of the two radicals
explanation: Benzyl radical is resonance stabilised (BDE of benzylic C-H ~90 kcal/mol); the 1° alkyl is not (~101).

question: Compare the stability of the two radicals
explanation: In the phenyl radical the unpaired electron is in an sp² σ orbital in the plane of the ring, orthogonal to the π system and not delocalised; the benzyl radical is delocalised.
trap: Phenyl radical is not resonance stabilised.

question: Which of the following radicals is stable enough to be observed in solution?
explanation: Gomberg (1900) observed triphenylmethyl radical, stabilised by delocalisation over three rings and steric protection from dimerisation.

question: Propene reacts with NBS (or Br2 at high T and low concentration) to give allylic bromide because
options: Vinylic C-H bonds are weaker than allylic C-H bonds
Br adds to the double bond reversibly
explanation: Abstraction of an allylic H gives the resonance stabilised allyl radical, which is far more stable than vinylic or 1° radicals.

question: Arrange the following alkenes
explanation: More alkyl groups on the C=C carbons (hyperconjugation; sp²-sp³ C-C bonds) means a more stable alkene: tetra > tri > di (trans) > mono > ethene.

question: Arrange the following alkenes
explanation: Heat of hydrogenation is larger for less stable alkenes: ethene (32.8) > but-1-ene (30.3) > cis-but-2-ene (28.6) > trans-but-2-ene (27.6 kcal/mol).

question: Arrange the following dienes (C5H8)
explanation: Conjugated dienes are stabilised by delocalisation (heat of hydrogenation ~54 vs ~60 kcal/mol); cumulated dienes are the least stable (~70).

question: If an alkyl group is introduced at a sp² carbon of ethene, the stability of the alkene
explanation: Alkyl substituents stabilise C=C through hyperconjugation and by bonding an sp² carbon to an sp³ carbon (stronger C-C bond).

question: If a phenyl group is introduced at a sp² carbon of propene, giving 1-phenylpropene (conjugated), the stability
explanation: Conjugation of the C=C with the aromatic ring lowers the heat of hydrogenation.

question: Compare the stability of the two alkenes
explanation: In cis-but-2-ene the two methyls are on the same side (steric strain ~1 kcal/mol); trans is more stable.

question: Compare the heat of hydrogenation of the two compounds
options: B: Twice the heat of hydrogenation of but-1-ene
explanation: Hydrogenation of 1,3-butadiene releases less than twice that of 1-butene because of delocalisation energy (~3.5 kcal/mol): 57 vs ~60.

question: Which of the following alkenes is highly unstable and cannot be isolated at room temperature (Bredt's rule)?
explanation: Bredt's rule: a double bond cannot be placed at a bridgehead of a small bicyclic system because the p orbitals cannot overlap in a planar manner (the strain in bicyclo[2.2.1]hept-1-ene is prohibitive). Norbornene has the double bond at C2=C3, not at the bridgehead.
trap: Cyclohexene, norbornene (hept-2-ene) are fine; the bridgehead alkene in the bicyclo[2.2.1] system is the violating one.

question: Which of the following alkenes is the most stable?
explanation: Trisubstituted alkene 2-methylbut-2-ene has most hyperconjugative interactions of the choices.

question: The number of hyperconjugative structures possible for propene $\ce{CH3-CH=CH2}$ is
explanation: Only the three α-C-H bonds of the CH3 group can hyperconjugate: 3 no-bond structures.

question: The number of hyperconjugative structures of the tert-butyl cation $\ce{(CH3)3C+}$ is
explanation: Three methyl groups × three α C-H bonds = 9.

question: Which of the following shows NO resonance?
explanation: In $\ce{CH2=CH-CH2-Cl}$ the Cl is separated from the C=C by an sp³ carbon; the lone pair and π bond are not conjugated.

question: Arrange the following alkenes
explanation: Number of α-hydrogens: tetramethylethylene (12), 2-methylbut-2-ene (9), 2-methylpropene (6), propene (3).

question: Arrange the following alkyl groups (as substituents $\ce{R-C6H4-X}$ in reactions studied by Baker and Nathan)
explanation: Baker–Nathan effect: the order of electron release by hyperconjugation is CH3 > CH3CH2 > (CH3)2CH > (CH3)3C, which follows the number of α-H, contrary to the +I order.
trap: The +I order is exactly the opposite: tert-butyl > isopropyl > ethyl > methyl.

question: Arrange the following aromatic hydrocarbons
explanation: Total resonance energies: phenanthrene ≈ 92, anthracene ≈ 84, naphthalene ≈ 61, benzene ≈ 36 kcal/mol.
trap: Per ring, benzene has more resonance energy than anthracene.

question: If two methyl groups are introduced at both ortho positions of N,N-dimethylaniline, the +M effect of the $\ce{-N(CH3)2}$ group on the ring
explanation: The bulky ortho methyl groups twist the NMe2 group out of the plane of the ring so the N lone pair cannot overlap with the π system (steric inhibition of resonance).

question: Compare the C-Cl bond length in the two compounds
explanation: Partial double-bond character from lone pair delocalisation (and sp² C) shortens C-Cl in chlorobenzene (1.70 Å) compared with chloroethane (1.77 Å).

question: Which statement about resonance is correct?
options: Resonance structures are in rapid equilibrium
Resonance hybrid is more stable than any single contributing structure
Atoms change their positions between resonance structures
Resonance energy is the energy of the least stable canonical form
explanation: Resonance structures differ only in electron distribution; the actual molecule is a hybrid more stable than any contributing structure.

question: Arrange the following groups
Arrange the following alkyl groups
explanation: +I effect increases with the number of alkyl groups on the attached carbon: tert-butyl > isopropyl > ethyl > methyl.

question: Arrange the following carboxylic acids
explanation: Greater -I of the halogen on the α-carbon stabilises the carboxylate: pKa FCH2COOH 2.66 < ClCH2COOH 2.86 < BrCH2COOH 2.90 < ICH2COOH 3.17 < CH3COOH 4.76.

question: Arrange the following carboxylic acids
explanation: More Cl atoms mean more -I: pKa 0.65 (Cl3C), 1.29, 2.86, 4.76.

question: Arrange the following groups
explanation: -I effect depends on the s-character of the carbon bonded to the rest: sp (-C≡CH) > sp² (-CH=CH2) > sp³ (-CH2CH3).

question: If the chlorine atom of 2-chlorobutanoic acid is shifted to the C-4 position (4-chlorobutanoic acid), the acid strength
explanation: The inductive effect falls rapidly with distance along the carbon chain; pKa: 2-chloro 2.84, 3-chloro 4.06, 4-chloro 4.52.

question: When one H of acetic acid is replaced by a methyl group (propanoic acid), the acid strength
explanation: The +I methyl increases electron density on the carboxylate, destabilising it (pKa 4.76 → 4.87).

question: Compare the acid strengths
explanation: Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine, so CF3COOH (pKa 0.23) is stronger than CCl3COOH (0.65).

question: Which of the following is the strongest acid?
explanation: Two Cl on the α-carbon (pKa 1.29) beats one F (2.66).

question: Which of the following is aromatic?
explanation: The cyclopropenyl cation is planar, cyclic, fully conjugated with 2π electrons (4n+2, n=0). Cyclopentadienyl cation (4π) is antiaromatic; cycloheptatrienyl anion (8π) is antiaromatic; COT is non-planar and non-aromatic.

question: Which of the following is antiaromatic?
explanation: Cyclobutadiene is planar, cyclic, conjugated with 4π electrons (4n), hence antiaromatic.

question: Azulene, a blue bicyclic hydrocarbon (fused five- and seven-membered rings), is
explanation: Azulene has 10 π electrons (4n+2, n=2) in a planar bicyclic system and is aromatic; its dipole moment (~1.0 D) arises from the polarised form of cyclopentadienyl anion fused with tropylium cation.

question: Which of the following annulenes is aromatic?
explanation: [18]Annulene has 18 π electrons (4n+2, n=4), is planar and diatropic. [4] and [8] are antiaromatic/non-planar; [16] has 4n π.

question: Which of the following is NOT aromatic?
explanation: Cyclopentadiene has an sp³ CH2 in the ring, so conjugation is not continuous.

question: Arrange the following five-membered heterocycles with benzene
explanation: Resonance energy (kcal/mol): benzene 36 > thiophene 29 > pyrrole 21 > furan 16; the lower the electronegativity of the heteroatom the better its lone pair delocalises.

question: Arrange the following C7H7 species
explanation: Cation has 6π (aromatic), radical 7π (non-aromatic), anion 8π (antiaromatic if planar).

question: If two electrons are added to cyclooctatetraene (COT) forming $\ce{C8H8^2-}$, the stability
explanation: The dianion is planar with 10π electrons (4n+2) so it is aromatic; COT itself is non-planar with 8π.

question: If one CH of benzene is replaced by N (pyridine), its aromaticity
explanation: The N contributes one π electron, as does each CH; the lone pair is in an sp² orbital in the plane, so the sextet is unchanged.

question: Compare the stability of the two ions
explanation: Cyclopentadienyl anion is aromatic (6π); cyclopentadienyl cation is antiaromatic (4π).

question: In pyrrole and pyridine, which nitrogen lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet?
explanation: In pyrrole the N lone pair is in a p orbital and contributes 2π electrons; in pyridine it lies in an sp² orbital in the plane of the ring.
